dataset.name: Data for Machado-Silva et al. (2024), "Short-Term Groundwater Level Fluctuations Drive Subsurface Redox Variability"
description: This dataset contains the analytical data reported in Machado-Silva et al. (2024) as part of the COMPASS-FME project, which seeks to advance a scalable, predictive understanding of the fundamental biogeochemical processes, ecological structure, and ecosystem dynamics that distinguish coastal terrestrial-aquatic interfaces from the purely terrestrial or aquatic systems to which they are coupled.

The dataset consists of water quality parameters as well as redox potential, water content, and electrical conductivity. These data were collected in 2022 in Crane Creek (CRC), Portage River (PTR), and Old Woman Creek (OWC). Each of these sites included uplands (UP), transitions (TR), wetland-transition edge (WTE), and wetland (W) zones. The sites represent replicates of the Lake Erie terrestrial-aquatic interface under fluctuating water levels and are located in well-preserved areas with natural or restored marsh and forest cover.
This dataset consists of a single data file (Machado_Silva_et_al_2024_EST_data.csv) that is in comma-separated value (CSV) format. No special software is required to read it.
This dataset uses the ESS-DIVE Hydrologic Monitoring Reporting Format 1.0.

spatialCoverage.description: Old Woman Creek (OWC); one of the COMPASS-FME synoptic sites located within the Old Woman Creek lacustuary, 2.8 miles (4.5km) east of Huron, Ohio. This site is owned by the Ohio Department of Natural Resources (ODNR), managed by ODNR’s Division of Natural Areas & Preserves as Old Woman Creek National Estuarine Research Reserve. This site consists of four plots: upland ("UP"; located at 41.3763N, 82.5070W), transition ("TR"; 41.3758N, 82.5063W), wetland transition edge ("WTE"; 41.3760N, 82.5071W), and wetland ("W"; 41.3761N, 82.5078W). The site was established in December 2021.

Portage River (PTR); one of COMPASS-FME synoptic sites located on the shoreline of the Portage River lacustuary of southwestern Lake Erie, at the confluence of the Portage and Little Portage rivers, 5.25 miles (8.5 km) east of Oak Harbor, Ohio. This site is owned by the USFWS and managed as a part of the Ottawa National Wildlife Refuge complex. This site consists of three plots: upland ("UP"; located at 41.5015N, 83.0461W), transition ("TR"; 41.5020N, 83.0456W), and wetland ("W"; 41.5016N, 83.0444W). The site was established in December 2021.

Crane Creek (CRC); one of COMPASS-FME synoptic sites within the Crane Creek lacustuary region of southwestern Lake Erie, 9.25 miles (14.9 km) northwest of Oak Harbor, Ohio. This site is owned by the USFWS and managed as a part of the Ottawa National WIldlife Refuge complex. This site consists of three plots: upland ("UP"; located at 41.6153N, 83.2297W), transition ("TR"; 41.6219N, 83.2381W), and wetland ("W"; 41.6219N, 83.2389W). This site was established in December 2021.

measurementTechnique: Our study was conducted along the shoreline of the western and central basin of Lake Erie, which experiences significant fluctuations in water levels due to weather events, river inflows, seiches, and storm surges. We focused on three sites: Crane Creek (CRC), Portage River (PTR), and Old Woman Creek (OWC), including uplands (UP), transitions (TR), wetland-transition edge (WTE), and wetland (W) zones. The sites represent replicates of the Lake Erie terrestrial-aquatic interface under fluctuating water levels and are located in well-preserved areas with natural or restored marsh and forest cover.

Geologically, the area is characterized by middle Paleozoic sedimentary rock and soils formed by fine-textured lacustrine deposits and glacial until with variable-sized materials. Lithostratigraphy showed that wetlands are consistently formed by clay, uplands by silty clay at the top, and until below 1.7 m, while transitions exhibited variable intermediate conditions such as silty clay and until, silty clay and clay, or silty clay.

In December 2022, we installed three groundwater wells at each site by using a hand auger. The wells were 4.2 cm diameter PVC tubes with 2.5 mm slots at 1 cm intervals in the bottom 1.52 m and lid on top (ESP Supply), sealed on ground with bentonite. Each well was equipped with a vented multiparameter water quality sonde (Aquatroll 600, In-Situ) measuring groundwater oxidation–reduction potential (ORP), pH, temperature, electrical conductivity, dissolved oxygen (DO), water density, and barometric pressure at 15 min intervals.

Groundwater level (GWL, m) was calculated using the relationship between fluid potential and hydraulic head referred to the soil surface. Then, barometric pressure (P, kg m–1 s–1), groundwater density (ρ, kg m–3), gravity (g, m s–2), and depths of pressure sensors were measured during the sondes deployment. Groundwater oxidation–reduction potential (ORP) values were standardized to the Standard Hydrogen Electrode (SHE) using an equation derived from empirical measurements of commonly used reference electrodes versus SHE at different temperatures.

We standardized Eh values to a common pH to enhance the comparability of groundwater data from various locations and times. The adjustment was made using the following equation:
𝐸h′(mV)=𝐸h(mV)+[(pH−7)×59]
where Eh′ represents the Eh value adjusted to the reference pH, enabling the likelihood of a particular redox state as follows: oxidizing (Eh ≥ 400 mV), weakly reducing (200 mV ≤ Eh < 400 mV), moderately reducing (−100 mV ≤ Eh < 200 mV), and strongly reducing (Eh < −100 mV). (7,39) Then, we counted the number of 15 min observations and calculated the relative frequency of each associated redox state to total observation within zones and water level periods.
Full methodological details are given in Machado-Silva et al. (2024).
